intro: Siena lies on three hills in the middle of Tuscany, between the vineyards of Chianti and the bare clay hills of the Crete Senesi. For three centuries it was a free republic, a banking town that rivalled Florence, and it has kept its Gothic centre of brick almost as it was in the 14th century, round the shell of the Piazza del Campo. Twice every summer its seventeen contrade race the Palio there.

The Monte dei Paschi, the oldest bank in the world still in business

overview: Siena’s centre lies on three ridges that meet at a hollow, and the Piazza del Campo fills that hollow. From it the three main streets, Banchi di Sopra, Banchi di Sotto and Via di Città, climb along the ridges to the three thirds of the town, the terzi, and between them steep lanes and stairs drop into the valleys. Almost everything is built of the same brick, in the reddish brown of the earth round Siena that gave the paint colour burnt sienna its name.

Instant Siena takes you through the heart of it: down Banchi di Sopra to the Loggia della Mercanzia, into the Campo below the Torre del Mangia, up the Casato to the cathedral and Santa Maria della Scala, and back past the Baptistery and along Via delle Terme. The centre has been closed to cars since the 1960s. The real town climbs and falls on every street, but the game keeps it flat.
setting: Siena is the capital of its province in the south of Tuscany, about 70 kilometres south of Florence. To the north lie the hills and vineyards of Chianti, to the south-east the bare grey hills of the Crete Senesi and the Val d’Orcia, and to the west the woods of the Montagnola. The Via Francigena, the pilgrims’ road from Canterbury to Rome, runs right through the town.

The town has no river. For its water it dug the bottini, some 25 kilometres of tunnels under the hills that still feed its old fountains. Its summers are hot and dry and its winters cool, with the odd frost and now and then some snow.

history.title: From Saena Julia to a free town
text: Legend says that Senius, a son of Remus, founded Siena, which is why the she-wolf feeding the twins stands on columns all over the town. The Romans had a small colony here, Saena Julia, but the town only grew in the Middle Ages, as a stop on the Via Francigena.

By the 12th century Siena governed itself as a commune, and its merchants and bankers lent money to popes and kings across Europe. In 1260, at Montaperti, its army beat Florence, the great rival to the north, in one of the bloodiest battles of the time.

history.title: The Nine and the Black Death
text: From 1287 to 1355 the government of the Nine, merchants and bankers, ran the town in its best years. They paved the Campo, built the Palazzo Pubblico and the Torre del Mangia, brought water through the bottini and had Simone Martini and the Lorenzetti brothers paint the town hall. In 1339 they began a cathedral that would outdo Florence’s.

The plague of 1348 killed much of the town, Ambrogio Lorenzetti probably among them. The new cathedral was never finished, and Siena never quite grew back to its old size, which is why its medieval centre survived.

history.title: Saint Catherine and the Monte dei Paschi
text: Catherine Benincasa, a wool dyer’s daughter from the quarter of Fontebranda, became a mystic and a peacemaker, wrote to popes and princes, and urged the pope to leave Avignon and return to Rome. She died in 1380 and was made a saint in 1461.
In 1472 the town set up the Monte dei Paschi to lend money to the poor without usury. It has worked without a break ever since, the oldest bank in the world.

history.title: Under Florence, and in Italy
text: In 1554 the army of Florence and of the emperor Charles V laid siege to Siena. The town gave in in April 1555 after a year of hunger, and in 1557 it passed to Cosimo I de’ Medici, who built the Fortezza to keep it quiet. It stayed part of the Grand Duchy of Tuscany until Tuscany joined Italy in 1860.
For the next centuries Siena was a quiet provincial town, which kept its Gothic streets as they were. In 1995 UNESCO put its historic centre on the World Heritage List.

today: Siena is a university town and the seat of the Monte dei Paschi, with some 53,000 people and far more visitors. The centre is closed to cars, and the buses stop at the edge of it, by La Lizza and the Fortezza.

Life still turns on the contrade: each has its own church, fountain, museum and club, baptises its children a second time at its own fountain and eats together in the street in summer. On 2 July and 16 August the Campo fills up for the Palio, and on other days the town sits on its bricks with an ice cream or a glass of Chianti.
